title: Alcohol and Estrogen: How Drinking Changes Your Hormone Levels
excerpt: Does alcohol raise estrogen? How drinking changes estrogen levels in women and men, what it means for breast cancer risk and HRT, and what you can do about it.
metaDescription: Does alcohol raise estrogen? How drinking affects estrogen in women and men, what it means if you take HRT, the breast cancer link, and what helps.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol tends to raise estrogen levels. That has been seen in women before menopause, in women after menopause, and in men who drink heavily. For a light social drinker, the change from one or two drinks is small and short-lived. The effect gets more meaningful with regular drinking, with heavy drinking, and for people taking oral estrogen as hormone therapy. It matters mostly because estrogen helps drive some breast cancers, which is one of the reasons alcohol is linked to breast cancer risk at fairly modest amounts. This guide explains how alcohol pushes estrogen up, what the research actually shows, what it means if you're on HRT, what it means for men, and what you can reasonably do about it.

**The quick takeaways:** One drink doesn't "flood" you with estrogen. The research shows modest rises in blood estrogen with regular moderate drinking, and bigger effects in people on oral estrogen and in heavy drinkers with liver damage. Breast cancer risk climbs gradually with every extra drink per day, with no clearly safe threshold. If you take HRT, birth control, tamoxifen, or an aromatase inhibitor, ask your prescriber how alcohol fits in. If you're a man noticing breast tissue growth, that deserves a doctor visit, not a supplement.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research. It isn't a substitute for a doctor who knows your history and medications. **See a doctor if** you notice a new breast lump, nipple discharge, or skin changes on the breast (in any sex); you're a man with new breast swelling or tenderness, shrinking testicles, or low sex drive; you have irregular, very heavy, or missing periods; you're on hormone therapy and having bleeding you didn't expect; or you have signs of liver trouble such as yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or a swollen belly. If you drink heavily every day, don't stop suddenly without talking to a doctor, because alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous. Shaking, sweating, confusion, seeing things, or a seizure after cutting back is an emergency: call 911.

## What Estrogen Does and Why Alcohol Affects It

Estrogen isn't one hormone. It's a family. The main ones are **estradiol** (the strongest, and the dominant form before menopause), **estrone** (the main form after menopause), and **estriol** (mostly important in pregnancy). Everyone makes estrogen, including men. In women of reproductive age, most of it comes from the ovaries. After menopause, and in men, most estrogen is made in other tissues, especially fat, by an enzyme called **aromatase**, which converts testosterone and related hormones into estrogen.

Estrogen does a lot more than run the menstrual cycle. It helps keep bones strong, affects cholesterol and blood vessels, influences mood and sleep, and keeps skin and the vaginal lining healthy. It also stimulates the growth of breast tissue, which is why too much estrogen exposure over a lifetime is tied to breast cancer risk.

The link with alcohol runs largely through the **liver**. Your liver is the main place estrogen gets broken down and cleared, and it's also the main place alcohol gets broken down. When the two compete for the same machinery, estrogen can stay in circulation longer or get converted into its stronger form. Our guide on [how alcohol is metabolized](/never-hungover/how-alcohol-is-metabolized) covers the alcohol side of that process in more detail.

## How Alcohol Raises Estrogen: The Mechanisms in Plain Words

Researchers have proposed several routes. More than one is probably at work, and which one matters most depends on how much and how often you drink.

### 1. Alcohol changes the liver's chemical balance

When your liver breaks down alcohol, it uses up a helper molecule called NAD+ and turns it into NADH. A night of drinking shifts the liver's balance heavily toward NADH. That matters because the enzymes that convert estradiol (the strong form) into estrone (the weaker form) depend on that same balance. With the balance tilted, less estradiol gets converted, so more of the strong form stays in your blood. This is one of the better-supported explanations for the short-term rise in estradiol seen after drinking, especially in women taking estrogen as medication.

### 2. Alcohol can increase aromatase activity

Aromatase is the enzyme that turns androgens (testosterone and similar hormones) into estrogen. Studies in animals and in people with heavy drinking histories suggest alcohol can boost aromatase activity, particularly in the liver. More aromatase means more of your testosterone gets converted into estrogen. This is one reason men who drink heavily can end up with lower testosterone and higher estrogen at the same time.

### 3. A damaged liver clears estrogen more slowly

This one mainly applies to long-term heavy drinking. When alcohol has damaged the liver, as in fatty liver, alcoholic hepatitis, or cirrhosis, the liver can't break down and clear hormones as efficiently. Estrogen builds up. In men with alcohol-related cirrhosis, doctors have long recognized the visible signs of this: breast tissue growth, shrinking testicles, loss of body hair, and red spider-like blood vessels on the skin.

### 4. Alcohol can raise other hormones that feed estrogen

Controlled studies have found that alcohol can raise levels of DHEA sulfate, an adrenal hormone that the body can convert into estrogen and testosterone. That adds another source of raw material.

### 5. Plant estrogens in some drinks (a minor factor)

Hops, used in beer, contain plant compounds with weak estrogen-like activity, including one called 8-prenylnaringenin. Bourbon and some wines contain similar compounds in tiny amounts. In practice, the amounts in ordinary beer are small, and there's no good evidence that they meaningfully raise estrogen in typical drinkers. The alcohol itself is the much bigger player. The idea that "beer makes men grow breasts because of hops" is mostly a myth. When heavy beer drinkers do develop breast tissue, alcohol's effects on the liver, testosterone, and body fat are far more likely causes.

## What the Research Actually Shows

This topic has been studied for decades, mostly because of the alcohol and breast cancer link. Here is what the main lines of evidence say, without overstating any of it.

**Controlled feeding studies in postmenopausal women.** In a well-known US government study published in the *Journal of the National Cancer Institute* in 2001, researchers led by Joanne Dorgan carefully controlled what postmenopausal women ate and drank for weeks at a time. They gave the women no alcohol, about one drink a day, or about two drinks a day. Blood levels of estrone sulfate (a reservoir form of estrogen) and DHEA sulfate rose with the alcohol, and rose more with two drinks than one. The changes were modest, but they were measurable and dose-dependent, which is what you'd expect if alcohol is genuinely pushing estrogen up.

**Controlled studies in premenopausal women.** An earlier study from the same research group, published in the same journal in 1993, gave premenopausal women about two drinks a day for several menstrual cycles and found higher levels of some estrogens compared with when they didn't drink. Other studies in women who still have periods have found similar patterns, with some evidence that the effect is most noticeable around ovulation. Results haven't been perfectly consistent, partly because estrogen swings so much across the cycle that small effects are hard to measure.

**Women taking oral estrogen.** A small study published in *JAMA* in 1996 gave postmenopausal women a dose of alcohol roughly equal to a few drinks. Among women taking oral estradiol as hormone therapy, blood estradiol rose sharply after the alcohol. Among women not taking hormones, it didn't change much. This is the clearest evidence that alcohol interacts with estrogen *medication*, and it's the main reason the HRT section below exists.

**Large population studies.** Many observational studies, which track what people do and measure their hormones, have found that women who drink more tend to have higher estrogen levels on average. These studies can't prove alcohol is the cause, because drinkers can differ from non-drinkers in other ways. But combined with the controlled studies above, the overall picture is consistent.

**Men.** Studies in men are mostly of heavy drinkers. Long-term heavy drinking is linked to lower testosterone and, in many cases, higher estrogen, especially once the liver is affected. For moderate drinking in healthy men, the hormone effects are smaller and less consistent.

The fair summary: alcohol raises estrogen, the effect grows with the amount you drink, and it's strongest in people on oral estrogen and in heavy drinkers with liver damage. For someone having a couple of drinks a week, the hormonal change is small.

## Alcohol, Estrogen, and Breast Cancer

This is the part that matters most for health, and it's worth being straightforward about.

Alcohol is classified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), part of the World Health Organization, as a **Group 1 carcinogen**, meaning there is enough evidence that it causes cancer in humans. Breast cancer is one of the cancers it is linked to. In January 2025, the US Surgeon General issued an advisory on alcohol and cancer risk that highlighted breast cancer as one of the cancers where risk rises even at relatively low levels of drinking.

A large pooled analysis by the Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer, published in the *British Journal of Cancer* in 2002, combined data from dozens of studies. It found that breast cancer risk rose by roughly 7% for each additional 10 grams of alcohol per day, which is a bit less than one US standard drink. That's a relative increase, so for an individual woman it translates to a small absolute change in risk from a drink a day. But it adds up with heavier drinking, and there's no level at which the line clearly goes flat.

Higher estrogen is one of the main proposed reasons. Many breast cancers are **hormone receptor-positive**, meaning estrogen helps them grow, and the alcohol link appears stronger for these types in a number of studies. Estrogen isn't the only route, though. Alcohol is broken down into **acetaldehyde**, which damages DNA directly, and alcohol can also interfere with how cells use folate, a vitamin involved in DNA repair.

What this means in practice:

- **Less is lower risk.** There's no "safe" amount for breast cancer risk, but the risk at one or two drinks a week is much smaller than at two drinks a day.
- **Pattern matters less than total.** The risk is tied mostly to how much you drink on average over years, not whether it happens on weekends or spread across the week. Binge drinking carries its own separate risks, of course.
- **Your baseline matters.** If you have a family history of breast cancer, a known gene such as BRCA1 or BRCA2, dense breasts, or a personal history of breast cancer, it's worth having a specific conversation with your doctor about alcohol.

## Alcohol and HRT (Hormone Replacement Therapy)

If you're taking estrogen for menopause symptoms, alcohol deserves more thought than it does for someone who isn't.

### Why HRT changes the picture

The 1996 *JAMA* study described above found that alcohol sent estradiol levels much higher in women taking **oral** estradiol than in women not on hormones. Pills containing estrogen pass through the liver before reaching the rest of the body (this is called first-pass metabolism). Alcohol changes how the liver handles that estrogen, so more of the active form may end up in your blood after drinking.

**Transdermal estrogen** (patches, gels, and sprays) is absorbed through the skin and skips that first trip through the liver. It's reasonable to expect alcohol to have less of this specific effect with skin-based estrogen, but there's much less research on it, so nobody can say for sure how big the difference is.

### HRT, alcohol, and breast cancer risk

Combined HRT (estrogen plus a progestogen) is associated with a small increase in breast cancer risk with longer use. Alcohol is also associated with breast cancer risk. Some observational studies suggest the two together may add more risk than either alone, though the data are less clear than for either factor by itself. This is not a reason to panic about a glass of wine. It's a reason to factor your drinking into the HRT conversation with your doctor, especially if you drink most days.

### Practical points if you're on HRT

- **Tell your prescriber how much you actually drink.** It's genuinely relevant to choosing the type and dose of HRT, and to how often your risk is reviewed.
- **Ask whether patch or gel versus pill makes a difference for you.** Skin-based estrogen has some other advantages too, including a lower risk of blood clots than pills, which your doctor may already be weighing.
- **Watch for symptoms alcohol can worsen.** Many women find drinking triggers hot flashes and night sweats and makes menopause-related sleep problems worse. See our guide on [hot flashes after drinking](/never-hungover/hot-flashes-after-drinking) for why that happens.
- **Don't stop or change your HRT on your own** because of anything you read here. Ask first.

### Other hormone medicines worth asking about

- **Birth control pills.** Alcohol doesn't make the pill less effective. Vomiting within a few hours of taking it can, though, so a night of drinking that ends in being sick is the real risk. Follow the missed-pill instructions on your pack if that happens.
- **Tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors** (such as anastrozole, letrozole, and exemestane) are used to treat or prevent hormone-sensitive breast cancer by blocking estrogen or cutting its production. Because alcohol pushes estrogen the other way, many oncologists advise people on these drugs to keep drinking low. Ask your oncology team for their specific advice.

For a broader look at how alcohol interacts with common prescriptions, see our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications).

## Alcohol and Estrogen in Men

Men make estrogen too, mostly by converting testosterone through aromatase in fat and other tissues. Healthy men need some estrogen for bone strength, libido, and sperm production. Problems come when the balance tips too far.

### What heavy drinking does

Long-term heavy drinking hits male hormones from several directions at once:

- **It lowers testosterone.** Alcohol is directly toxic to the cells in the testicles that make testosterone, and it disrupts the brain signals that tell them to make it.
- **It can raise estrogen.** More aromatase activity and, later, a damaged liver that can't clear estrogen both push estrogen up.
- **It adds body fat.** Alcohol is calorie-dense, and belly fat is rich in aromatase. More fat means more testosterone converted to estrogen, which can feed further fat gain.

The result can be **gynecomastia** (growth of real breast tissue, which feels firmer than fat), lower sex drive, erectile problems, and reduced fertility. In men with advanced alcohol-related liver disease, these changes are common and well documented.

### What about moderate drinking?

For a healthy man having a few drinks a week, the effects on estrogen are small. Studies of short-term drinking show testosterone can dip for a while after a heavy session, then recover. The hormone story mostly becomes a real concern with regular heavy drinking, not occasional social drinking. Our guide to [alcohol and testosterone](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-testosterone) goes deeper on the male side, including how much drinking it takes before levels shift.

### When men should see a doctor

New breast swelling or tenderness in a man is worth getting checked. Most cases have harmless causes, and some medicines (certain heartburn, prostate, and heart drugs, and anabolic steroids) can cause it too. But it can occasionally signal a hormone problem, liver disease, or, rarely, male breast cancer. A doctor can tell the difference and run simple blood tests.

## Does Alcohol Affect Estrogen Across the Menstrual Cycle?

Estrogen rises and falls through the month: lower during your period, climbing to a peak just before ovulation, then a second smaller rise in the second half of the cycle. Some studies suggest alcohol has its biggest effect on estrogen around ovulation, when levels are already high, though findings are mixed.

What's clearer is that regular heavier drinking can disrupt the cycle itself. It's linked with irregular periods, cycles where you don't ovulate, and worse premenstrual symptoms in some women. Light drinking usually doesn't have a noticeable effect. If you've noticed your periods changing around nights out, our article on whether [alcohol affects your period](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-affect-your-period) covers that in detail.

A practical note: many women find their tolerance seems to change across the month. Research on whether alcohol is processed faster or slower at different cycle phases has been inconsistent, so there's no good evidence for a reliable "safe week" to drink more. Women generally reach higher blood alcohol levels than men from the same drink because of differences in body size and body water, and that's true throughout the cycle.

## Is "Estrogen Dominance" From Alcohol Real?

You'll see a lot of online content claiming alcohol causes "estrogen dominance" and selling supplements to fix it. Some clarity:

- **"Estrogen dominance" isn't a formal medical diagnosis.** It's a wellness-industry term that's used loosely to describe almost any symptom, from bloating to mood swings.
- **Alcohol does raise estrogen**, as described above, but for a social drinker the change is modest and doesn't usually produce symptoms on its own.
- **Real hormone problems have real tests.** If you have symptoms you're worried about, such as very heavy periods, breast changes, or unexplained weight changes, a doctor can measure your hormones and look for actual causes such as thyroid problems, polycystic ovary syndrome, fibroids, or medication effects.
- **"Liver detox" products to clear estrogen** are mostly marketing. Your liver already does this job, and the best thing you can do for it is drink less. Our guide to [liver detox methods versus marketing myths](/never-hungover/best-liver-detox-science-based-methods-vs-marketing-myths-2025) covers this.

## What You Can Do

If the alcohol and estrogen link concerns you, these are the steps with the best support:

1. **Drink less on average.** This is the single most effective lever. Because the breast cancer link follows total intake, cutting from a drink a day to a few a week makes a real difference over years.
2. **Have alcohol-free days.** These give your liver a break and naturally bring down your weekly total.
3. **Keep body fat in a healthy range.** After menopause and in men, fat tissue is the main estrogen factory. Alcohol calories make this harder.
4. **Eat fiber and vegetables.** Fiber helps the body excrete estrogen through the gut. A diet rich in vegetables, beans, and whole grains is a sensible baseline anyway.
5. **Talk to your doctor if you're on hormones** or have a higher baseline breast cancer risk.
6. **Get breast changes checked**, in any sex, and keep up with recommended breast screening.

### What about DHM and other supplements?

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound studied for how it affects alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with a small amount of human data. Here's the honest part for this topic: **there is no good evidence that DHM changes estrogen levels or lowers the hormone-related risks of drinking.** It doesn't cancel out alcohol's link with breast cancer, and it's no reason to drink more. If you're on HRT, birth control, or a breast cancer drug, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement, because we have very little data on how supplements like DHM interact with hormone medicines. Our guide on [DHM and hormonal considerations for women](/never-hungover/dhm-women-hormonal-considerations-safety-2025) covers what's known.

If you drink socially and want to try DHM for the morning after, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. For habits that help most with how you feel the next day, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).
If you're in your 40s or 50s and alcohol has started hitting differently, hormone shifts may be part of it. Our guide to [perimenopause and alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/perimenopause-alcohol-intolerance) covers why tolerance often drops during that stage.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol raises estrogen levels through the liver's chemistry, more aromatase activity, and, in heavy drinkers, slower clearance by a damaged liver.
- The effect is small for light social drinkers and grows with the amount you drink.
- It's strongest in people taking oral estrogen and in heavy drinkers with liver damage.
- Higher estrogen is one reason alcohol is linked to breast cancer, and that risk rises steadily with average daily intake, with no clearly safe threshold.
- If you're on HRT or another hormone medicine, tell your prescriber how much you drink.
- In men, heavy drinking can lower testosterone, raise estrogen, and cause breast tissue growth. New breast changes in anyone are worth a doctor visit.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol increase estrogen?**

Yes. Controlled studies in premenopausal and postmenopausal women have found that regular drinking raises blood estrogen levels, and the rise gets bigger with more alcohol. Heavy drinking can also raise estrogen in men. For a light social drinker the change is modest and short-lived. The effect is larger in people taking oral estrogen and in heavy drinkers whose liver has been damaged.

**How does alcohol raise estrogen levels?**

Breaking down alcohol shifts the liver's chemical balance in a way that slows the conversion of estradiol (the strong form of estrogen) into weaker forms. Alcohol may also boost aromatase, the enzyme that turns testosterone into estrogen, and it can raise adrenal hormones the body converts into estrogen. In long-term heavy drinkers, a damaged liver clears estrogen more slowly, so it builds up.

**Is it safe to drink alcohol while on HRT?**

Many women on hormone therapy drink in moderation, but it's worth discussing with your prescriber. A small study in JAMA found alcohol raised estradiol levels much more in women taking oral estrogen than in women not on hormones. Both HRT and alcohol are also linked to breast cancer risk. Tell your doctor how much you drink, ask whether a patch or gel might suit you better, and don't change your HRT on your own.

**Does alcohol raise estrogen in men?**

Heavy drinking can. It lowers testosterone, may increase the conversion of testosterone into estrogen, adds aromatase-rich belly fat, and, once the liver is damaged, slows estrogen clearance. This can cause breast tissue growth (gynecomastia), low sex drive, and erectile problems. For a healthy man having a few drinks a week, the effect on estrogen is small. New breast swelling in a man should be checked by a doctor.

**Does beer contain estrogen?**

Beer contains plant compounds from hops with weak estrogen-like activity, such as 8-prenylnaringenin, but the amounts in ordinary beer are small. There's no good evidence they meaningfully raise estrogen in typical drinkers. When heavy beer drinkers develop breast tissue or hormone changes, the alcohol's effects on the liver, testosterone, and body fat are far more likely causes than the hops.

**How is alcohol linked to breast cancer?**

Alcohol is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the WHO's cancer agency, and breast cancer is one of the cancers it's linked to. A large 2002 pooled analysis found risk rose by roughly 7% for each extra 10 grams of alcohol a day, a bit under one US standard drink. Higher estrogen is one proposed reason, along with DNA damage from acetaldehyde, a by-product of alcohol. There is no clearly safe threshold, but less drinking means lower risk.

**Does alcohol make birth control less effective?**

No, alcohol itself doesn't reduce how well the pill works. The real risk is vomiting within a few hours of taking a pill, which can stop it from being absorbed. If that happens after a night of drinking, follow the missed-pill instructions in your pack or ask a pharmacist.

**Can DHM lower estrogen or offset alcohol's hormone effects?**

There is no good evidence that DHM changes estrogen levels or reduces alcohol's link with breast cancer. DHM has been studied mainly for alcohol metabolism and liver health, mostly in animals with limited human data. If you take HRT, birth control, or a breast cancer medicine, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.
